{{h|FOURTH ADHYÂYA.}}

{{sh|{{sc|{{Anchor+|Khanda1|First Kha''nd''a}}.}}}}

1. Next comes the Sûdadohas<ref>The Nishkevalya-''s''astra is represented in the shape of a bird, consisting of trunk, neck, head, vertebrae, wings, tail, and stomach. Before describing the hymns which form the neck, another hymn has to be mentioned, called Sûdadohas, which has to be recited at the end of the hymns, described before, which form the trunk. Sûdadohas is explained as 'yielding milk.' and because that word occurs in the verse, the verse is called Sûdadohas. It follows on the Nada verse, Rv. VIII, 69, 3. Cf. Ait. Âr. I, 5, 1, 7.</ref> verse. Sûdadohas is breath, and thereby he joins all joints with breath.

2. Next follow the {{sp|neck}} verses. They recite them as Ush''n''ih, according to their metre<ref>They occur in another ''s''âkha and are to be recited such as they are, without any insertions. They are given by ''S''aunaka, Ait. Âr. V, 2, 1.</ref>.

3. Next comes (again) the Sûdadohas verse. Sûdadohas is breath, and thereby he joins all joints with breath.

4. Next follows the {{sp|head}}. That is in Gâyatrî verses. The Gâyatrî is the beginning of all metres<ref>It was created from the mouth of Pra''g''âpati.</ref>; the head the first of all members. It is in Arkavat verses (Rv. I, 7, 1-9)<ref>They are called so, because the word arka occurs in them.</ref>. Arka is Agni. They are nine verses. The head consists of nine pieces. He recites the tenth verse, and that is the skin and the hairs on the head. It serves for reciting one verse more than (the nine verses contained in) the Stoma<ref>The chanters of the Sâma-veda make a Triv''ri''t Stoma of this hymn, without any repetitions, leaving out the tenth verse. The reciters of the Rig-veda excel them therefore by reciting a tenth verse. This is called ati''s''a''m''sanam (or -nâ).</ref>.
